questions.q: Why can't an LLM simply be retrained constantly to stay current?
options: It would violate the model's license agreement
Training a frontier model takes significant time and compute, so it can't realistically happen continuously
Retraining is instant and cheap, so this isn't actually a limitation
Models are not capable of being retrained more than once
questions.explain: Full retraining is a months-long, resource-intensive process, which is exactly why every deployed model is already somewhat out of date by the time it ships.

questions.q: If the information an LLM needs easily fits inside the prompt, what does this lesson recommend?
options: Split it into chunks and embed it regardless of size
Always fine-tune the model on it instead
Just include it directly in the prompt rather than building a retrieval pipeline for it
Build a vector database first, then evaluate whether it was needed
questions.explain: Standing up embeddings and a vector database for content that would fit directly in a prompt is unnecessary complexity for a problem that doesn't require it.

questions.q: What does fine-tuning actually change about a model?
options: The model's weights, by continuing training on your own examples
Nothing — it only changes what's in the prompt
The vector database the model queries
The model's maximum context window size
questions.explain: Fine-tuning continues the training process on new examples, which adjusts the model's internal weights directly.

questions.q: Why does this course cover embeddings and vector databases (Chapters 2-3) before the full pipeline (Chapter 4)?
options: Because chunking and prompt assembly are not actually part of RAG
Because embeddings and vector databases are the foundation retrieval quality depends on — if retrieval pulls back the wrong chunks, no prompting technique fixes a bad answer
Because the LLM generation step is optional and covered last
Alphabetical ordering of the topics
questions.explain: Poor-quality retrieval caused by a weak embedding model or a misconfigured vector store undermines every later step, so the course builds that foundation first.

questions.q: What is a text embedding, precisely?
options: A compressed ZIP archive of the original text
A dense numeric vector produced by a neural network, representing a piece of text's meaning as a point in high-dimensional space
A list of the most frequent words in a document
A hash value used only for detecting exact duplicate text
questions.explain: Embeddings are dense, meaning-bearing vectors, not compression artifacts, word-frequency lists, or hashes for exact matching.

questions.q: Using this lesson's formula (dimensions x 4 bytes), what is the approximate raw storage cost for one 1536-dimension embedding vector?
options: About 1.5 KB
About 60 KB
About 600 bytes
About 6 KB
questions.explain: 1536 dimensions x 4 bytes per float = 6,144 bytes, which is approximately 6 KB, as shown directly in the lesson's worked numbers.

questions.q: Why should hard constraints like data residency be applied before comparing model quality?
options: They can eliminate otherwise strong options (like a hosted API, if data can't leave your infrastructure) before quality even matters
Hard constraints are always the same as quality metrics
Hard constraints only apply to self-hosted models
Hard constraints are optional and can be skipped entirely
questions.explain: A constraint like 'data must stay on our infrastructure' rules out hosted APIs regardless of how well they score, so checking it first avoids wasted evaluation effort.

questions.q: Why do many vector databases default to dot product instead of cosine similarity?
options: Dot product is more accurate than cosine similarity in every case
Cosine similarity cannot be used for retrieval tasks
Once every vector is L2-normalized to length 1, dot product and cosine similarity produce identical rankings, and dot product is cheaper to compute
Dot product requires less storage space than cosine similarity
questions.explain: When vectors are pre-normalized to unit length, the magnitude term that distinguishes dot product from cosine similarity becomes irrelevant, so dot product gives the same ranking at a lower computational cost.

questions.q: In the worked RRF example in this lesson (k = 60), why does doc_B (dense rank 3, keyword rank 1) outscore doc_A (dense rank 1, keyword rank 4)?
options: Because doc_A was excluded from the sparse list entirely
Because doc_B appeared earlier alphabetically
Because RRF always favors the second document listed
Because doc_B ranked well in both lists, and RRF rewards consistently good ranking across multiple lists over being the single best result in only one
questions.explain: Computing the formula gives doc_B a combined score of about 0.0323 versus doc_A's about 0.0320 — RRF's summing behavior means strong-in-both beats best-in-one-only.

questions.q: In the Qdrant console screenshot shown in this lesson, what does the 'PUT collections/demo1' call do?
options: It deletes the demo1 collection
It lists every existing collection
It creates a new collection, setting its vector size and distance metric (Cosine) at that moment
It queries the collection for the nearest vectors to a specific input
questions.explain: The PUT request in the screenshot creates a new collection named demo1, explicitly configuring a vector size of 1 and a Cosine distance metric as part of that creation call.

questions.q: What does it mean that Chroma runs "embedded" by default?
options: It runs inside your own application process, with no separate database server to stand up
It requires a dedicated GPU server to operate
It only works inside a web browser
It can only store a fixed, small number of vectors
questions.explain: Embedded means the database runs in-process alongside your own code, which is what makes Chroma the fastest option to start prototyping with locally — no server to install or connect to.

questions.q: In HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World), how does a search generally proceed?
options: It assigns every vector to one of nlist clusters first
It converts every vector into text before comparing
It skips indexing entirely and always does an exact scan
It starts at a sparse top layer and greedily descends toward denser layers, narrowing in on the query at each step
questions.explain: HNSW builds a layered graph — sparse with long-range links at the top, dense with every vector at the bottom — and a search greedily moves toward the closest connected node, dropping a layer each time it can't get any closer.

questions.q: Why are retrieved chunks numbered (like [1], [2]) during prompt assembly?
options: Numbering is purely cosmetic and has no functional purpose
It gives each chunk a stable label the model can refer back to later, enabling citations
It sets the order chunks are embedded in
It determines each chunk's similarity score
questions.explain: A chunk needs a stable label assigned at assembly time so the model's answer can reference a specific source — this can't be added after the model has already responded.

questions.q: What does the 'with_payload' field do in a vector database search request?
options: It filters results by metadata
It sets the similarity distance metric
It requests that each result include its stored text and metadata, not just an ID
It increases the number of results returned
questions.explain: with_payload: true tells the vector database to return the stored text and metadata alongside each matched vector's ID and score.

questions.q: In the RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter example, what does chunk_overlap=50 do?
options: It discards the last 50 characters of every chunk
It limits the splitter to 50 chunks maximum
It repeats the trailing 50 characters of one chunk at the start of the next chunk
It sets the embedding dimensionality to 50
questions.explain: Overlap repeats a small trailing slice of text at the start of the next chunk so that content spanning a chunk boundary still appears in full in at least one chunk.

questions.q: What is the main risk of a large chunk size?
options: It becomes impossible to embed
It cannot be stored in a vector database
It often mixes several topics, so one relevant sentence can drag an otherwise-irrelevant chunk into the results
It always produces a lower embedding dimensionality
questions.explain: A large chunk is more likely to contain multiple unrelated topics, which reduces retrieval precision even when it carries more surrounding context.

questions.q: How does HyDE differ from multi-query RAG in its approach to the same underlying problem?
options: HyDE generates one hypothetical answer, while multi-query RAG generates several reformulated questions
HyDE only works with graph databases, while multi-query RAG only works with vector databases
HyDE requires no LLM call, while multi-query RAG requires three
HyDE eliminates the need for a vector database entirely
questions.explain: Both target the same terse-query, vocabulary-mismatch problem, but from opposite directions: HyDE closes the gap with one answer-shaped embedding, multi-query RAG closes it with several alternative question phrasings.

questions.q: What is the core difference between a standard RAG pipeline and agentic RAG?
options: Agentic RAG does not use an embedding model
In agentic RAG, retrieval is exposed as a tool the model decides whether and when to call, rather than a fixed step that always runs first
Agentic RAG skips prompt assembly entirely
Agentic RAG only works with graph databases
questions.explain: Standard RAG retrieves automatically before generation; agentic RAG lets the model itself decide whether retrieval is needed and whether to call it again.

questions.q: Why are results from multiple reformulations typically deduplicated by chunk ID?
options: Because vector databases reject duplicate search requests
Because deduplication increases the embedding dimensionality
Because the same genuinely relevant chunk is often retrieved by more than one reformulation
Because chunk IDs expire after one search
questions.explain: Since different reformulations aim at the same underlying intent, they frequently retrieve overlapping chunks, so deduplication avoids feeding the same chunk into the prompt multiple times.

questions.q: What does the example Cypher query in this lesson do?
options: It computes a cosine similarity score between two documents
It traverses relationships — Acme Corp's parent company, then sibling companies, then which of those have a disputed-with relationship — with no embedding involved
It re-ranks a list of retrieved chunks by relevance
It splits a document into chunks using a recursive separator list
questions.explain: The Cypher query is a structural pattern match over explicit relationships in the graph, not a similarity comparison over embedded vectors.

questions.q: In the worked tuning example, what combination of scores points at retrieval specifically, rather than generation?
options: Low faithfulness and low context_recall together
High faithfulness and low context_recall
Low faithfulness and high context_recall
High context_precision and low context_recall only when chunk_overlap is zero
questions.explain: Strong faithfulness means the model is using its context well; weak context_recall means the real answer wasn't retrieved in the first place — together, that isolates the problem to retrieval, not generation.

questions.q: What is the capstone project built across Lessons 29-31?
options: A production RAG knowledge assistant over a single, real knowledge base
A new embedding model trained from scratch
A general-purpose chatbot with no retrieval component
A vector database engine built from first principles
questions.explain: The capstone is scoped to one real knowledge base so every pipeline stage from the course has an actual, working job to do.

questions.q: In the full round trip example, what makes a citation like '[1]' in the model's answer traceable back to a real source?
options: The re-ranker assigns citation numbers directly
The chunk's doc_id and page metadata, captured back at ingestion and carried through to the numbered context in the prompt
The vector database automatically generates citation text
The embedding model stores citation numbers in the vector itself
questions.explain: A citation is only traceable because the chunk was stored with source metadata (Lesson 16) that survives through retrieval and into the numbered context assembled into the prompt.

questions.q: Which chapter does this lesson say became the capstone's actual pipeline build — ingestion through citations and failure handling?
options: Chapter 1 (Why RAG Exists)
Chapter 2 (Embeddings Deep Dive)
Chapter 4 (Building a RAG Pipeline)
Chapter 6 (Capstone) alone, with no connection to earlier chapters
questions.explain: Chapter 4 covered ingestion, retrieval, re-ranking, prompt assembly, citations, and failure handling — the exact stages wired together in the capstone build.
